title: Data and Central Tendency
lines: USAT-GS Statistics opens with the basics of handling data: what kind of variable you have, how data are classified and tabulated, how graphs are read, and how to find an average. Expect short calculations of the mean, median and mode, a weighted or combined mean, and questions on which average suits which data. All of it is HSSC Part I work, done by hand in about a minute.
## Kinds of data
- Qualitative variable (attribute): categories such as blood group, gender or province.
- Quantitative variable: numbers. Discrete if counted (children in a family, goals scored); continuous if measured (height, time, weight).
- Primary data are collected first-hand for your own inquiry; secondary data come from someone else's work, such as a published report.
- Scales: nominal (names only), ordinal (order, e.g. class positions), interval and ratio (equal units; ratio has a true zero).
## Classification and frequency tables
Data can be classified by time (chronological), by place (geographical), by attribute (qualitative) or by size (quantitative). A grouped frequency table needs a few terms:
| Term | Meaning | Example for 20–29
| Class limits | the numbers written | 20 and 29
| Class boundaries | limits moved half the gap outwards | 19.5 and 29.5
| Midpoint | (lower + upper) ÷ 2 | 24.5
| Class width | difference of boundaries | 10
- Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total. Cumulative frequency adds the frequencies from the top.
- Sturges' rule gives a rough number of classes: k = 1 + 3.3 log n.
## Graphs, described in words
- Histogram: bars on class boundaries with no gaps; area shows frequency. With unequal widths, height = frequency ÷ width.
- Frequency polygon: join the midpoints of the tops of the bars.
- Ogive: cumulative frequency plotted against upper boundaries; used to read off the median and quartiles.
- Pie chart: angle of a sector = (part ÷ total) × 360°.
! Bar charts have gaps between bars and suit categories; histograms have no gaps and suit continuous classes.
## The arithmetic mean
x̄ = Σx ÷ n for raw data and x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf for a frequency table, using midpoints for grouped classes. Shortcut with an assumed mean A: x̄ = A + Σ(x − A) ÷ n.
- Σ(x − x̄) = 0 always.
- If every value is changed to ax + b, the mean becomes a·x̄ + b.
- Combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂). Weighted mean = Σwx ÷ Σw.
> Example 1. Class A has 30 students with mean 60; class B has 20 with mean 70. Combined mean?
> Example 2. The mean of 20 numbers is 15, but 43 was copied for 34. Correct mean?
## Geometric and harmonic means
- G.M. of n values = nth root of their product; log G.M. = Σ log x ÷ n. It suits growth rates and ratios and fails if any value is zero.
- H.M. = n ÷ Σ(1/x). It suits average speed over equal distances and similar rates.
- For unequal positive values A.M. > G.M. > H.M.; for two numbers G.M.² = A.M. × H.M.
> Example 3. A van goes from Multan to Bahawalpur at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. Average speed?
> H.M. = 2 ÷ (1/60 + 1/40) = 2 ÷ (5/120) = 48 km/h. The tempting 50 km/h ignores that the slow leg takes longer.
## Median and mode
- Median: the middle value after sorting. For n values it is the ((n + 1)/2)th value; for even n, average the two middle values.
- Grouped median = L + (h/f)(n/2 − C), where L is the lower boundary of the median class, f its frequency, C the cumulative frequency before it and h the width.
- Mode: the most frequent value. Grouped mode = L + (f₁ − f₀)h ÷ [(f₁ − f₀) + (f₁ − f₂)], using the modal class and its neighbours.
- Empirical relation for moderately skewed data: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
> Example 4. Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5. Median?
> n/2 = 15; cumulative 5, 13, 25 puts the median in 20–30. Median = 20 + (10/12)(15 − 13) = 21.67.
## Choosing an average
| Average | Best for | Weakness
| Mean | numerical data without outliers | pulled by extreme values
| Median | skewed data such as incomes | ignores the size of extremes
| Mode | categories, e.g. favourite colour | may not exist or may not be unique
In a symmetrical distribution mean = median = mode. In positive skew (long right tail) mean > median > mode; in negative skew the order reverses.
! Sort the data before finding a median. Reading the middle of an unsorted list is the commonest slip.
! A combined mean is not the average of the two means unless the groups are the same size.
! Class limits and class boundaries are different: boundaries are used for widths, histograms and the median formula.
## Quick check
- Is the number of rooms in a house discrete or continuous?
- What is the midpoint of 40–49?
- Find the G.M. of 3 and 12.
- Which average would you use for shoe sales by colour?
